--- title: "R with tidymodels" description: "The seven steps most modelling pages in this course are built from, run once from start to finish on the coastal survey and explained line by line: split the stations, prepare the inputs, name the model, join the two, fit, predict and score." order: 1 categories: [toolkit] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Most models in the course are fitted in the same seven steps Most modelling pages in this course fit a model in R, and they follow the same seven steps: split the data, prepare the inputs, name the model, join the two, fit, predict and score. This page runs those steps once, on a small example, and says what each line does. Later pages change one or two lines at a time, so once these seven are familiar, the code on any page reads as a small variation on them. The steps come from **tidymodels**, a collection of R packages for fitting models. A **package** is a bundle of functions that someone has written and shared, loaded with `library()`. On its own, R gives almost every method its own way of being called; with tidymodels, a linear regression, a random forest and a neural network are all set up the same way. This page is an orientation, not a course in R. If R itself is new, the free book *R for Data Science* (in Further resources below) is the place to start. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## Three pieces of R syntax carry most of the code - `<-` stores a result under a name, so that later lines can use it. - A function is called with its inputs in brackets, and some are given by name: `round(3.14159, digits = 2)`. - `|>`, the **pipe**, passes the result on its left into the function on its right. Read it as "and then". ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} depths <- c(12, 40, 95) depths |> mean() |> round(digits = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 49 ``` ::: ::: The second line reads: take the depths, then average them, then round to one decimal place. Most code in the course is a chain like this one, one step per line. ## The idea A model is built in seven steps, and tidymodels has one function for each. The first holds back some of the data for checking the model at the end. The next three only *describe* the model: how to prepare the inputs, which method to use, and the object that holds both. Nothing is computed until the fifth step, `fit()`. That is what lets a page swap the method or the preparation without touching the rest of its code. ::: {.diagram} ![The seven steps of a tidymodels fit. The training set goes to `fit()` and the test set to `augment()`; the recipe, the model specification and the workflow only describe the model, so nothing is computed until `fit()`.](img/tidymodels-shape.svg){fig-alt="A flow of seven cards. Card 1, hold back a test set: initial_split() splits the data into a larger training set, three quarters, and a smaller test set, one quarter. A dashed box says steps 2 to 4 describe the model and nothing is computed yet; inside it, card 2, prepare the inputs: recipe() fills gaps and turns categories into numbers; card 3, name the model: linear_reg(), the method and its settings but no data; both lead into card 4, join the two: workflow() holds the recipe and the model. The training set and card 4 both lead into card 5, fit: fit(train) works out the medians, then fits the model, on the training set. Card 5 leads to card 6, predict: augment(test), which also receives the test set, prepares it the same way and predicts each station. Card 6 leads to card 7, score: rmse() compares the predictions with the recorded values. A note says the test set is used once, at the end, and nothing is learned from it."} ::: If you also read Python, the same steps carry these names: | Step | tidymodels | scikit-learn | | --- | --- | --- | | 1. Hold out a test set | `initial_split()`, `training()`, `testing()` | `train_test_split()` | | 2. Prepare the inputs | `recipe()` plus `step_*()` | `ColumnTransformer` plus transformers | | 3. Name the model | `linear_reg()`, `rand_forest()` | `LinearRegression()`, `RandomForestRegressor()` | | 4. Join the two | `workflow()` | `Pipeline` | | 5. Fit | `fit()` | `.fit()` | | 6. Predict | `augment()`, `predict()` | `.predict()` | | 7. Score | `rmse()` | `root_mean_squared_error()` | ## Worked example We predict the **abundance** of one species at each station, the number of animals counted there, from the station's depth, temperature, chlorophyll and seabed type. The outcome is a number, so this is a [regression](../chapters/01-introduction/types-of-learning.qmd). ### The split holds back a quarter of the stations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() set.seed(1) split <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) c(training = nrow(train), test = nrow(test)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> training test #> 600 200 ``` ::: ::: `load_coastal_survey_clean()` is one of the course's own functions: it reads the survey with its recording errors already fixed. `initial_split()` sets aside a random quarter of the stations as the **test set**; the other three quarters are the **training set**, the stations the model learns from. The test stations play no part until the end, so their score shows how the model does on stations it has never seen. The split is random, and `set.seed(1)` fixes the random draw, so the same stations land in each set every time the code runs. ### A recipe says how to prepare the inputs ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec <- recipe( abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + substrate, data = train ) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) ``` ::: The formula reads "abundance, predicted from depth, temperature, chlorophyll and substrate": the outcome goes on the left of `~` and the inputs, which tidymodels calls *predictors*, on the right. Each `step_*()` adds one instruction to the **recipe**: - Some stations have no chlorophyll reading, so `step_impute_median()` fills each gap with the median of the training stations. - Seabed type is a word (sand, mud, gravel or rock), and linear regression needs numbers, so `step_dummy()` turns it into columns of 0s and 1s, one for each type but the first. Nothing has been computed yet: the recipe is a list of instructions. The median is worked out later, from the training stations alone, so the test stations have no say in how the data are prepared. Filling the gaps across the whole survey first would let the test set [leak into the model](../chapters/02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd) and make its score look better than it is. ### A workflow joins the recipe to linear regression ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fitted <- workflow() |> add_recipe(rec) |> add_model(linear_reg()) |> fit(train) ``` ::: `linear_reg()` is a **model specification**: it names the method, linear regression, and holds no data. [Linear regression](../chapters/01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd) predicts the outcome as a starting value plus a fixed amount for each unit of each input. `workflow()` starts an empty workflow, `add_recipe()` and `add_model()` put the recipe and the model in, and `fit(train)` does the work: it runs the recipe on the training stations, then fits the model to the result. ### The predictions sit beside the recorded counts ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predictions <- augment(fitted, test) predictions |> select(abundance, .pred) |> head() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| abundance| .pred| |---------:|--------:| | 0| 2.868505| | 1| 2.551792| | 3| 6.144475| | 9| 7.296651| | 0| 1.484766| | 0| 3.368330|
::: ::: `augment()` runs the test stations through the fitted workflow, so their gaps are filled with the training median before the model predicts them. It returns the test set with a new column, `.pred`, beside the recorded `abundance`. `select()` keeps those two columns and `head()` shows the first six stations. ### RMSE scores the predictions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predictions |> rmse(truth = abundance, estimate = .pred) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|.metric |.estimator | .estimate| |:-------|:----------|---------:| |rmse |standard | 3.517815|
::: ::: The [RMSE](../chapters/01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd), or root mean squared error, is roughly how far a prediction usually lands from the recorded count, in animals. A number on its own says little, so set it beside the simplest prediction there is: the training stations' average count, the same at every test station. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predictions |> mutate(.average = mean(train$abundance)) |> rmse(truth = abundance, estimate = .average) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|.metric |.estimator | .estimate| |:-------|:----------|---------:| |rmse |standard | 3.872515|
::: ::: Linear regression misses by 3.52 animals at a typical test station, and predicting the average everywhere misses by 3.87. The model has learned something from the inputs, but counts of one species vary a lot from station to station, and much of that variation is left over. ## Changing the method takes one line The split, the recipe and the scoring stay as they are. Only the model specification changes, here to a random forest. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2) forest <- workflow() |> add_recipe(rec) |> add_model(rand_forest(mode = "regression")) |> fit(train) augment(forest, test) |> rmse(truth = abundance, estimate = .pred) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|.metric |.estimator | .estimate| |:-------|:----------|---------:| |rmse |standard | 3.58885|
::: ::: A [random forest](../chapters/03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd) averages the predictions of hundreds of decision trees, each grown on a different random sample of the training stations, so it can follow relationships that bend where linear regression draws straight lines. `mode = "regression"` tells it the outcome is a number, and `set.seed(2)` fixes its random samples. The forest misses by 3.59 animals, against 3.52 for linear regression. On this one split the two are close, and another split could put them the other way round. Telling whether one method really predicts better than another takes more than one split, and much of the course is about doing that well: [Cross-validation](../chapters/07-validation/cross-validation.qmd) compares models over many splits, and [Choosing a method](../chapters/03-supervised-learning/choosing-a-method.qmd) puts several side by side on the survey. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Most models in the course are fitted in the same seven steps: split, recipe, model specification, workflow, fit, predict and score. - A recipe and a model specification are instructions. Nothing is computed until `fit()`, and then only from the training set, so the test set stays out of the preparation. - The test set is used once, at the end, to show how the model does on stations it has never seen. - An RMSE means more beside a simple baseline, such as predicting the training average at every station. - Changing the method changes one line; the rest of the code stays as it is. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Swap `rand_forest(mode = "regression")` for `boost_tree(mode = "regression")` and rerun the last chunk. Which lines had to change? 2. Add `salinity_psu` and `season` to the recipe's formula. Does either model's RMSE change by more than the gap between the two models? 3. Change `set.seed(1)` before the split to `set.seed(2)` and rerun everything. Do the two models keep their order? ## Further resources **Documentation** - [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/), Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Garrett Grolemund. The free book for R itself: the pipe, data frames and plots, for readers new to the language. - [Get Started](https://www.tidymodels.org/start/), tidymodels. Five articles covering the same ground as this page, at more length. - [Tidy Modeling with R](https://www.tmwr.org/), Max Kuhn and Julia Silge. The book, free online. [Recipes](https://www.tmwr.org/recipes.html) and [resampling](https://www.tmwr.org/resampling.html) are the two chapters to read first. **Video** ::: {.video-list} - [![](../img/video/z57i2GVcdww.jpg){.video-thumb fig-alt="Get started with tidymodels and classification of penguin data, on YouTube" loading="lazy"}](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z57i2GVcdww) [Get started with tidymodels and classification of penguin data](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z57i2GVcdww), Julia Silge. The same steps as this page, worked live on a different dataset. - [![](../img/video/NTtcTF2tFEA.jpg){.video-thumb fig-alt="posit::conf(2023) Workshop: Introduction to tidymodels, on YouTube" loading="lazy"}](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NTtcTF2tFEA) [posit::conf(2023) Workshop: Introduction to tidymodels](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NTtcTF2tFEA), Posit PBC.
